title: How should a client respond when a competitor makes a move?
description: "How should the client respond to a rival's move?" A rival cuts prices, launches a product or enters the market.
hook: When a competitor makes a move, the client should size what is genuinely at risk before reacting, understand why the rival did it and whether it can keep it up, and then compare every response, including doing nothing, on the profit it protects. Matching a price cut across the board is often the most expensive option. Here is the structure and a worked example that shows why.
body:
When you will use it

Use it when a rival cuts prices, launches a product, enters the client's market or changes the rules of the game, such as a discounter opening nearby or a new technology arriving. It is a decide question: "how should we respond?" You test the options, put a number on each, and end with a clear choice. See which framework to use for each type of question for the other families.

Ask this first

What exactly did they do, and which of our customers does it touch?

A 20% price cut on one product in one region is a different problem from a national price war. Pin down the scope before you size anything.

The structure

  • How exposed are we?
    • Customers at risk, by segment
    • Revenue and contribution at risk
  • Why are they doing it, and can they keep it up?
    • Which segments they are targeting
    • Their costs and funding: a short promotion or a permanent shift?
  • Our options
    • Do nothing
    • Defend the customers at risk: loyalty offers, contracts, service
    • Respond on price or product: match, part-match, upgrade
    • Change the game: copy their offer under a separate brand, partner or buy

Make it your own

Size the threat before choosing a response, and compare every option with doing nothing. Doing nothing is a real option, and it is right when little profit is at risk. Think one move ahead too: if the client matches, how will the rival respond? A rival with lower costs can win a price war it started.

A short worked example

A rival cuts its price on a product from $100 to $80. The client sells 100,000 units a year at $100, with a variable cost of $60 a unit. The figures are illustrative.

Today: 100,000 × ($100 − $60) = $4.0M of contribution.

Now suppose research suggests about 20% of customers (20,000) would switch if the client does nothing. Compare three responses:

ResponseWorkingContribution
Match for everyone100,000 × ($80 − $60)$2.0M
Hold the price80,000 × $40$3.2M
Targeted offer at $80 to 30,000 at-risk customers30,000 × $20 + 70,000 × $40$3.4M

Matching across the board is the worst option: it gives away $20 on every unit, including to the 80,000 customers who were never going to leave. The targeted offer is best, assuming the 30,000 includes the 20,000 would-be switchers and keeps them. It reaches more customers than are really at risk because no client can identify switchers perfectly.

Find the break-even. Holding the price beats matching unless the client would lose more than $2.0M of contribution, which is $2.0M ÷ $40 = 50,000 customers, or half its base. That is the number to test. If the rival's product is genuinely better, losses could approach that, and a product response would matter more than price.

Check the rival. If its costs are similar to the client's, it earns $20 a unit at $80, half of what it made before. It may not keep that up for long, which strengthens the case for a targeted, temporary response.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer reacts:

We should match their price straight away so we don't lose customers.

A strong answer sizes first:

Matching for everyone halves our contribution to $2M. Holding the price only loses that much if half our customers leave, so I'd target a retention offer at the segments most at risk and watch what the rival does next.

The mistakes to avoid

  1. Matching immediately. It is often the most expensive response.
  2. Ignoring "do nothing". Every option should beat it on profit.
  3. Forgetting the rival's economics. Can it sustain the move, and how will it react to yours?
  4. Thinking only about price. Contracts, service and product upgrades can defend customers more cheaply.

Practise with real prompts

1. A rival has cut prices 20% on our best-selling product. How do we respond?

Show the answer
  • The threat: what exactly did they cut, where and for how long? Can their costs sustain it?
  • Impact on us: customers lost so far and at risk; profit at risk under each scenario.
  • Our options: match, part-match, hold, differentiate; target only the customers at risk.
  • Their likely reaction: risk of a price war; how long each side can keep it up.

Where to start: impact. How many customers actually switch before we react?

The trap: matching immediately without sizing what is really at risk.

2. How should an electricity company respond to the growth of rooftop solar?

Show the answer
  • Impact: lost demand and revenue, though customers still need the grid at night and in winter.
  • Defend: pricing (fixed charges against per-kWh), regulation and grid fees.
  • New services: selling and installing solar and batteries, EV charging, home energy management.
  • Costs: grid and plant costs as demand falls; closing or selling plants no longer needed.

Where to start: how much revenue is at risk, and how fast.

The trap: only fighting solar through tariffs instead of also selling it.

3. A shampoo brand has lost 4 points of market share in a year.

Show the answer
  • Where share went: to which rivals or own-label brands, in which channels and stores.
  • Price: our price gap against rivals; how often we promote.
  • Product and brand: rivals' launches, our advertising and awareness.
  • Distribution: shelf space, out-of-stocks, online visibility.

Where to start: where the share went. Losing to own-label suggests a price problem; losing to a rival's launch suggests a product problem.

The trap: spending more on advertising before knowing who took the share.
